provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that due process requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before terminating parental rights, and that a fair-preponderance standard is unconstitutional.
key_cases.relevance: It is the federal constitutional floor for the burden of proof in every Minnesota termination of parental rights case.
key_cases.quote: Evaluation of the three Eldridge factors compels the conclusion that use of a "fair preponderance of the evidence" standard in such proceedings is inconsistent with due process.

key_cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of R.W.
key_cases.holding: The court held that parental rights may not be terminated on best interests alone without at least one statutory ground, but affirmed the termination because statutory grounds were established by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Minnesota rule that a statutory ground proven by clear and convincing evidence is a precondition to termination, best interests alone never sufficing.
key_cases.quote: the court of appeals ignored the clear statutory directive that parental rights cannot be terminated in the absence of at least one statutory ground for termination

key_cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of S.E.P.
key_cases.holding: Reinstating the termination, the court held that appellate courts closely examine the record to confirm the evidence was clear and convincing, and that the findings on statutory grounds, reasonable efforts and best interests were not clearly erroneous.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court's statement of the appellate standard applied to a termination of parental rights.
key_cases.quote: But we closely inquire into the sufficiency of the evidence to determine whether it was clear and convincing.

key_cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Child of R.D.L.
key_cases.holding: The court held that the statutory presumption of palpable unfitness applied to parents whose rights to another child were previously involuntarily terminated is narrowly tailored to a compelling state interest and does not violate equal protection.
key_cases.relevance: It upholds the presumption that drives many Minnesota terminations against parents with a prior involuntary termination.
key_cases.quote: We therefore hold that the statute does not violate the equal protection provisions of the United States or Minnesota Constitutions

key_cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of A.I.
key_cases.holding: The court held that a parent's murder of the children's mother, carrying a prison sentence longer than the children's remaining minority, satisfies the statutory definition of palpable unfitness, and affirmed the termination.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Minnesota rule for terminating the rights of an incarcerated parent whose sentence outlasts the children's minority.
key_cases.quote: appellant's act of murdering the children's mother, resulting in a prison sentence longer than the children's remaining age of minority, satisfies the statutory definition of palpable unfitness

key_cases.case_name: In re Welfare of Children of S.R.K.
key_cases.holding: The court held that ICWA and MIFPA require qualified expert witness testimony as part of the court's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt determination that continued parental custody is likely to cause serious emotional or physical damage, and affirmed the terminations.
key_cases.relevance: It sets the heightened beyond-a-reasonable-doubt and qualified-expert-witness requirements that govern termination of parental rights to an Indian child in Minnesota.
key_cases.quote: The statute provides that the court's serious-damage determination must be supported by evidence "including testimony of qualified expert witnesses."

state_agency.name: Minnesota Department of Children, Youth, and Families
state_agency.hotline: No statewide hotline. Call the county or Tribal child protection agency where the child lives — the directory link is on dcyf.mn.gov/individuals-and-families/report-abuse

extended_foster_care_age: To age 21 (voluntary; youth must meet one of five eligibility conditions; re-entry to 21 allowed; Minn. Stat. § 260C.451)

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Must file TPR or document compelling reason

timeline_requirements.starts_from: The child's placement out of the home of the parent or guardian from whom the child was removed
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Minn. Stat. § 260C.204; subd. 1 requires the court to hold the permanency progress hearing no later than six months after the child's placement, and subd. 4(a)(2) lets the court continue the matter no more than six additional months before a hearing under §§ 260C.503 to 260C.521.
